title: Text embeddings and semantic search
summary: How a transformer becomes a sentence embedding model (pooling, normalization, contrastive training with in-batch negatives) and how to search with it: vector indexes, ANN, hybrid BM25 fusion and re-ranking.
outcomes: Explain why bi-encoders make search over millions of passages feasible where cross-encoders do not
Compute a masked mean-pooled, normalized sentence vector and explain why cosine equals dot product for unit vectors
Compute the in-batch contrastive loss for a small batch and explain the role of the scale and hard negatives
Estimate memory and compute for exact vector search and explain what ANN indexes and Matryoshka embeddings trade away
Design a hybrid retrieve and re-rank pipeline and compute a reciprocal rank fusion

lessons.title: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow

blocks.md:
From the prerequisite course you know an **embedding**: a learned map from an item to a vector, trained so that related items land close together. This course applies that idea to whole sentences and passages, and uses it to search. First, the problem it solves.

**Lexical search** such as BM25 scores a document only by the query words it contains. That is fast and precise, but it is blind to meaning: two texts that say the same thing with different words share no terms and get no credit.

blocks.prompt: The DPR paper gives this example. Query: *Who is the bad guy in lord of the rings?* Passage: *Sala Baker is best known for portraying the villain Sauron in the Lord of the Rings trilogy.* Which query words can a keyword matcher use to find this passage?
blocks.reveal: Only *lord* and *rings* (plus stopwords like *the* and *of*, which carry almost no weight). The words that carry the question, *bad guy*, never appear: the passage says *villain*. Any page about Lord of the Rings film locations matches just as well. A dense retriever can learn that *bad guy* and *villain* mean the same thing and place them close together.

blocks.md:
One fix is a **cross-encoder**: feed the query and the passage together into a transformer such as BERT and have it output one relevance score. Because attention runs across both texts, it is accurate. The catch is cost: every (query, passage) pair needs its own full forward pass, and nothing can be computed ahead of time.

The Sentence-BERT paper quantifies this. Finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences means scoring every pair:

blocks.caption: About 50 million BERT inferences, which the SBERT paper reports as roughly 65 hours.

blocks.md: The alternative is a **bi-encoder** (SBERT calls it a siamese network): one encoder turns each text into a vector **on its own**, and relevance is a cheap vector similarity such as cosine. Each of the 10,000 sentences is encoded once (about 5 seconds in the SBERT paper), and all pairwise cosines then take about 0.01 seconds. For search, the passage vectors are computed once, offline, and reused for every query.

scenes.caption: Cross-encoder: query and passage enter the model together, so attention compares every query token with every passage token. Accurate, but there is nothing to reuse between pairs.
Scoring a new passage against the same query means a full forward pass again. For N passages, that is N passes per query.
Bi-encoder: each text is encoded separately by the same network into a fixed-length vector. Relevance is just a cosine between two vectors.
The passage vector never depends on the query, so it is computed once offline and stored. At query time only the short query is encoded.

blocks.title: Model calls to find the closest pair among n texts

scenes.caption: Both axes are logarithmic. The cross-encoder grows quadratically, the bi-encoder linearly. At 10,000 texts the gap is about 5,000x in forward passes; the cosines left over for the bi-encoder are cheap arithmetic.

blocks.md: A bi-encoder trades accuracy for speed in one specific way: the passage vector cannot look at the query. In exchange, every passage is encoded once, ahead of time, and search becomes a nearest-neighbor lookup among vectors. Everything else in this course follows from that trade.

Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

blocks.question: You must rank 1,000,000 passages for each incoming query. Which cost profile describes a pure cross-encoder versus a bi-encoder at query time?
options: Both need 1,000,000 forward passes per query; the bi-encoder just uses a smaller model
Cross-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes per query. Bi-encoder: 1 forward pass for the query plus 1,000,000 vector similarities
Cross-encoder: 1 forward pass per query. Bi-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes
Both need 1 forward pass, because attention handles all passages at once
blocks.explain: The cross-encoder has to read the query together with every passage, so its work scales with the corpus on every query. The bi-encoder encoded the passages offline; online it encodes only the query and then does cheap dot products, which an index can speed up further.

blocks.question: Which property is what makes the bi-encoder's precomputation possible?
options: Its passage vector is a function of the passage alone
It uses cosine instead of dot product
It is a smaller model than a cross-encoder
It tokenizes the query and passage with the same vocabulary
blocks.explain: Precomputation needs the passage representation to be independent of the query. Cosine versus dot product, model size and vocabulary are all irrelevant to that; a cross-encoder can share vocabulary and still cannot precompute anything.

lessons.title: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine

blocks.md:
A transformer encoder such as BERT reads a text and outputs **one vector per token**, each already mixed with context from the other tokens. Search needs **one vector per text**, of a fixed length regardless of how long the text is. The step that collapses token vectors into one is called **pooling**.

Sentence-BERT tried three options: take the output at the special `[CLS]` token, take the mean of all token vectors (MEAN), or take the per-dimension max (MAX). Its default is MEAN; the widely used all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model also uses mean pooling.

There is one trap. Texts are processed in batches, and a batch must be rectangular, so short texts are padded with `[PAD]` tokens. The encoder still produces output vectors at padding positions, and they are not zero. The **attention mask** (1 for real tokens, 0 for padding) tells pooling which rows to average.

Toy example (simplified to 4 dimensions; real models use 384 or 768): the text *cheap flights* becomes `[CLS] cheap flights [SEP]`, padded with two `[PAD]` tokens to match a longer neighbor in the batch.

blocks.title: Token output vectors for cheap flights, padded to 6

scenes.caption: The encoder outputs a 4-number vector for each of the 6 positions, including the two padding positions. Their values are made up for this toy example.
The attention mask is 1 for the four real tokens and 0 for padding. Masked mean pooling averages only the highlighted rows.
Forgetting the mask averages all six rows, so the padding vectors pull the result toward [-0.5, -0.2, 0.6, 0.5].

blocks.title: Pooling, then normalizing to unit length

scenes.caption: Masked mean: sum the four real rows and divide by 4.
Divide by the length 0.566 to get a unit vector. This is the sentence embedding; its length is now 1.
Without the mask: sum all six rows and divide by 6. Padding drags every dimension.
Normalized, the unmasked vector has cosine 0.682 with the correct one. Same sentence, different vector, only because of what else was in the batch.

blocks.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F

def mean_pool(token_embeddings, attention_mask):
    # token_embeddings: (batch, seq_len, dim); attention_mask: (batch, seq_len)
    mask = attention_mask.unsqueeze(-1).float()
    summed = (token_embeddings * mask).sum(dim=1)
    counts = mask.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1e-9)
    return summed / counts

emb = mean_pool(outputs.last_hidden_state, batch["attention_mask"])
emb = F.normalize(emb, p=2, dim=1)  # unit length: dot product == cosine
blocks.caption: Masked mean pooling then L2 normalization, the same steps shown on the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card.

blocks.md: To compare two embeddings, the standard measure is **cosine similarity**: the dot product divided by both lengths, so only the direction counts. It ranges from -1 to 1. If both vectors are already unit length, cosine and dot product are the same number, which is why systems normalize once at indexing time and then use the cheaper dot product.

blocks.prompt: Query $q=(1,0)$. Document $a=(0.8,0.6)$ has length 1. Document $b=(3,4)$ has length 5. Which one ranks first by dot product, and which by cosine?
blocks.reveal: Dot product: $q\cdot a = 0.8$, $q\cdot b = 3$, so **b** wins. Cosine: $0.8/1 = 0.8$ for a and $3/5 = 0.6$ for b, so **a** wins. Dot product rewards length; cosine ignores it. Neither is wrong: use the one the model was trained with. DPR, for example, trained with dot product, while SBERT used cosine.

blocks.md: Does any pretrained transformer give good sentence embeddings if you just mean-pool it? The SBERT paper tested this on semantic textual similarity (STS) benchmarks, measuring how well the cosine between two sentence vectors ranks sentence pairs the way human annotators did (Spearman correlation, times 100).

blocks.title: Average STS Spearman correlation (SBERT paper, Table 1)

scenes.caption: Off-the-shelf BERT, unfine-tuned: averaging its token vectors scores 54.81 and the [CLS] vector 29.19, both worse than simply averaging GloVe word vectors (61.32).
The same BERT, fine-tuned as a siamese bi-encoder on sentence pairs (SBERT-NLI-base), reaches 74.89, above the earlier dedicated sentence encoders.

blocks.md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

blocks.question: Your service embeds documents in batches of 32. The same document gets clearly different vectors depending on which batch it lands in. What is the most likely bug?
options: The model is non-deterministic because of dropout at inference
Cosine similarity is unstable for vectors of length 1
Mean pooling is averaging over padding positions instead of using the attention mask
The tokenizer lowercases differently per batch
blocks.explain: Padding length depends on the longest text in the batch, so if pooling ignores the attention mask, the number and effect of [PAD] rows changes with batch composition. Dropout is disabled in eval mode, and tokenization does not depend on the batch.

blocks.question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
blocks.explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

blocks.md:
To make cosine meaningful, train on **pairs** that should be close: a question and the passage that answers it, a title and its abstract, two paraphrases. The training signal is a ranking: query $q_i$ should be closer to its own passage $p_i$ than to other passages.

Where do the other passages come from? The DPR paper uses a cheap trick called **in-batch negatives**. Take a batch of $B$ pairs, encode the $B$ queries and $B$ passages, and compute all $B \times B$ similarities $S = QP^\top$. The diagonal entries are the correct pairs; every off-diagonal entry is a free negative. Each query gets $B-1$ negatives without encoding anything extra.

blocks.caption: Softmax cross-entropy over each row of the similarity matrix, with the diagonal as the correct class. s is the scale (1 / temperature).

blocks.md:
This is the same loss known as InfoNCE (from contrastive predictive coding). In the sentence-transformers library it is `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, which uses cosine similarity with a default **scale** $s = 20$, equivalent to a temperature of 0.05. Its docstring notes values between 10 and 100 are common, and that with dot product you would set the scale to 1.

Worked example, $B = 4$ (numbers are a made-up snapshot early in training):

blocks.title: In-batch similarities, then row softmax at scale 20

scenes.caption: Cosine similarities between 4 queries and the 4 passages in the batch. The diagonal holds the true pairs; the 12 off-diagonal cells are free negatives.
Each row goes through softmax(20 x cosine). Row q1 puts 0.98 on its own passage. Losses per row are -ln of the diagonal: 0.019, 0.226, 0.027, 0.160, mean 0.108.
Row q2 is the hard case: p3 has cosine 0.48, close to the true 0.55, so p3 still gets 0.20 of the probability. Most of the gradient in this batch comes from here and from q4 vs p1.

blocks.prompt: Keep row q2 (cosines 0.30, 0.55, 0.48, 0.12) but use scale 1 instead of 20. What probability does the softmax give the correct passage p2?
blocks.reveal: Only **0.30**, against 0.28 for p3. Cosines live in [-1, 1], so differences of 0.07 barely move a softmax at scale 1, and the loss stays above 1.1 for every row (1.212 here; the maximum, a uniform guess, is $\ln 4 = 1.386$). Scaling by 20 turns the 0.07 gap into a logit gap of 1.4, giving 0.80 vs 0.20. The scale sets how sharply the model is pushed to separate positives from near misses.

blocks.title: Row q2 softmax: scale 1 versus scale 20

scenes.caption: Scale 1: the distribution is almost flat, since the logits are the raw cosines 0.30, 0.55, 0.48, 0.12.
Scale 20: the same cosines become logits 6, 11, 9.6 and 2.4. The true passage gets 0.80; the hard negative keeps 0.20; the easy ones are near 0.

blocks.md:
Why does this matter for which negatives you use? The gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to a negative's logit is that negative's probability $p_j$. An **easy negative** with $p_j \approx 0$ teaches almost nothing. A **hard negative**, one that looks relevant but is not, carries most of the signal.

DPR therefore added one **BM25 hard negative** per question: a passage that scores high for the question's keywords but does not contain the answer. Each such passage is shared as a negative by every question in the batch.

blocks.title: DPR ablation: top-20 retrieval accuracy (NQ dev, Table 3)

scenes.caption: Same 7 gold negatives per question, but taken from the current batch instead of sampled from the whole training set: 63.1 to 69.1. In-batch reuse adds many more training pairs for free.
Bigger batches mean more negatives per query (7, 31, 127): 69.1, 70.8, 73.0. Accuracy rises steadily with batch size.
Adding one BM25 hard negative per question at batch 128 jumps to 78.0. DPR reports that a second BM25 negative did not help further.

blocks.md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

blocks.question: DPR trains with batch size 128 and one BM25 negative per question, shared across the batch. How many negative passages does each question see?
blocks.explain: 127 in-batch gold passages from the other questions, plus all 128 BM25 negatives in the batch (each question's BM25 negative is shared with everyone). DPR's table lists this configuration as 127+128.

blocks.question: After some training, every off-diagonal cosine in a batch is below 0.1 while every diagonal is above 0.8. The loss is near zero, but retrieval on real queries is still mediocre. What is the most useful change?
options: Lower the scale to 1 so the loss becomes larger
Remove normalization so vectors can grow
Add hard negatives such as BM25 results that do not contain the answer
Shrink the batch so each step is faster
blocks.explain: Random in-batch negatives have become too easy, so their gradient ($p_j$) is near zero. Hard negatives restore signal on exactly the near misses the model gets wrong at search time. Lowering the scale only flattens the softmax, and a smaller batch gives fewer negatives.

lessons.title: Searching a corpus: indexing, ANN and vector size

blocks.md:
With a trained bi-encoder, semantic search is two separate pipelines.

- **Offline (indexing):** split documents into passages that fit the model's input limit, encode each passage, normalize, and store the vectors in an index alongside passage ids.
- **Online (query):** encode the query with the same model, compute similarity to stored vectors, and return the top $k$.

The input limit is real: the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card says text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated, so anything beyond that is silently ignored unless you chunk. DPR split Wikipedia into 100-word passages, giving 21,015,324 of them.

scenes.caption: Offline: every passage goes through the encoder once. For DPR this took about 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs for 21 million passages.
Online: only the query is encoded. Its vector is compared with stored vectors and the best k ids come back.
The query must use the same model (and the same prefix or prompt convention) as the passages. Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces.

blocks.md: A toy run, simplified to 3 dimensions so you can check it by hand. The query is *who is the bad guy in lord of the rings*, embedded and normalized to $(0.777, 0.621, 0.104)$. Five passages are already normalized in the index; each score is a dot product of unit vectors, so it is the cosine.

blocks.title: Toy corpus: cosine with the query

scenes.caption: Dot products of unit vectors. D1 shares almost no words with the query yet scores highest; D4 is unrelated and scores near 0.
Top-2 retrieval returns D1 and D2. Exact search had to score all 5 passages to know that.

blocks.md: Exact (brute-force) search scores every stored vector: $N \times d$ multiply-adds per query. That is fine for small corpora; the sentence-transformers docs suggest a plain implementation up to about 1 million entries. At DPR's scale it is not:

blocks.caption: Compute and float32 memory for exact search over DPR's Wikipedia index.

blocks.md:
**Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** indexes trade a little recall for a lot of speed. A popular one is **HNSW** (hierarchical navigable small world): a stack of proximity graphs where each vector appears on a random number of layers, with exponentially fewer vectors on higher layers. A search starts at the sparse top layer, greedily walks toward the query, and drops down layer by layer, which gives roughly logarithmic scaling.

DPR used FAISS with an HNSW index on CPU and reports 995 questions per second (top 100 each), against 23.7 per second per CPU thread for BM25 in Lucene. The price is paid offline: building the HNSW index took 8.5 hours, versus about 30 minutes for Lucene's inverted index.

Short queries and long passages are an **asymmetric** search task. Many models are trained with role prefixes and expect them at inference: E5 says every input should start with `query: ` or `passage: `. sentence-transformers exposes `encode_query` and `encode_document`, which apply a model's configured prompts. Omitting the prefix a model was trained with quietly hurts recall.

Memory scales with dimension, so smaller vectors are tempting. **Matryoshka Representation Learning** trains one embedding so that its first $m$ dimensions work on their own, by adding the training loss at several nested sizes (for BERT-base, 12, 24, 48 up to 768). You can then keep only a prefix. This works only for models trained this way; truncating an ordinary embedding throws away information it spread across all dimensions.

scenes.caption: Each float32 dimension costs 4 bytes: 768 dims is 3,072 bytes per vector, 3.07 GB per million.
Keeping Matryoshka prefixes halves storage and per-query compute at each step. Renormalize the prefix before using dot product, since a truncated unit vector is no longer length 1.

blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # 384 dims
passages = ["Sala Baker played the villain Sauron in the Lord of the Rings.",
            "Hobbits eat several meals a day."]
corpus = model.encode_document(passages, convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)

query = model.encode_query("who is the bad guy in lord of the rings",
                           convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)
hits = util.semantic_search(query, corpus, top_k=2, score_function=util.dot_score)
print(hits[0])  # [{'corpus_id': ..., 'score': ...}, ...]
blocks.caption: Exact search with sentence-transformers. With normalized vectors, dot_score equals cosine. Swap util.semantic_search for an ANN index (FAISS, hnswlib) at large scale.

blocks.question: You will store 10 million passages as 384-dimensional float32 vectors. Roughly how much memory do the raw vectors need?
options: 1.5 GB
3.8 GB
blocks.explain: 10,000,000 x 384 x 4 bytes = 15,360,000,000 bytes, about 15.4 GB, before any index overhead such as HNSW graph links. 3.8 GB would be 1 byte per dimension; 30.7 GB would be 768 dimensions.

blocks.question: To save memory, an engineer keeps only the first 128 dimensions of a standard (non-Matryoshka) 768-dim embedding model and sees recall collapse. Why?
options: 128 dimensions is below the minimum HNSW supports
Truncation changes the tokenizer
Cosine similarity is undefined for 128-dim vectors
The model never learned to pack the most useful information into the first dimensions; only Matryoshka-trained models do
blocks.explain: An ordinary embedding spreads information across all dimensions, with no ordering. Matryoshka training adds the loss at nested prefix sizes so each prefix is useful by itself. HNSW and cosine work at any dimension.

blocks.question: With an E5 model, queries are embedded with the `query: ` prefix, but the corpus was indexed last year with no prefix at all. What should you expect?
options: Weaker retrieval, because passages were embedded without the passage prefix the model expects
No effect: the prefix only matters at training time
An error, because the vectors have different dimensions
Better retrieval, because mixing conventions adds diversity
blocks.explain: The model card instructs that each input start with query: or passage:, and the model was trained that way. The vectors still have the same dimension, so nothing crashes; quality degrades silently. Re-embed the corpus with the right prefix.

lessons.title: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking

blocks.md: Dense retrieval is not a strict upgrade over keywords. The DPR authors observed the two fail differently: BM25 is sensitive to highly selective keywords and phrases, while DPR captures lexical variation and semantic relationships but may lack capacity for **salient phrases that appear rarely**, such as names, product codes or error strings. On SQuAD, where annotators wrote questions while looking at the passage and so reused its words, BM25 beat DPR.

blocks.prompt: A support search indexes error-log passages. A user types `ERR_SSL_VERSION_INTERFERENCE`. Which retriever is more likely to put the exact matching passage first: BM25 or a general-purpose dense bi-encoder?
blocks.reveal: **BM25.** The string is a rare, highly selective token sequence; an exact match gets a large IDF (inverse document frequency) weight, because very few passages contain it. A dense model compresses the whole text into one vector, and a code it rarely saw in training may land near other SSL errors that look similar. This is why production systems often run both.

blocks.md: The gap shows up at scale, too. **BEIR** evaluated retrievers zero-shot (no training on the target data) across 18 datasets and found BM25 a robust baseline: dense retrievers were efficient but often underperformed it out of domain, while re-ranking and late-interaction models (which compare query and passage token vectors) scored best at high compute cost. E5 later reported being the first model to beat BM25 on BEIR zero-shot without any labeled data. **MTEB** (8 task types, 58 datasets in its first release) found that no single embedding method dominates across all tasks. The practical rule: measure on your own queries before trusting a leaderboard.

**Hybrid search** runs BM25 and dense retrieval in parallel and merges the ranked lists. Their raw scores live on different scales, so a common merge uses ranks only: **reciprocal rank fusion** (RRF), from Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (SIGIR 2009). A document's fused score sums $1/(k+\text{rank})$ over the lists it appears in, with $k = 60$, a value the authors fixed in a pilot study.

blocks.title: Reciprocal rank fusion of two top-4 lists (scores x 1000)

scenes.caption: BM25 ranks P7 first (it contains the exact error code). The dense retriever ranks P2 first. P2 and P9 appear in both lists.
P2: 1/(60+2) + 1/(60+1) = 32.52 thousandths. P9: 1/63 + 1/63 = 31.75. Showing up in both lists beats being first in only one.
P7, first in BM25 only, gets 1/61 = 16.39 and stays in the top 3. P4 and P1 tie at 1/64 = 15.63.

blocks.md: The last stage brings back the accuracy the bi-encoder gave up. A **retrieve and re-rank** pipeline takes a modest candidate list (the sentence-transformers docs use about 100) from BM25, dense or hybrid retrieval, then scores each candidate with a **cross-encoder** that reads query and passage together. Running the expensive model on 100 passages is affordable; on 21 million it is not. DPR's own QA system did this: its reader re-scored the retrieved passages with cross-attention.

scenes.caption: Two cheap first-stage retrievers run in parallel. BM25 catches exact rare terms; the bi-encoder catches paraphrases and synonyms.
RRF merges by rank, so the two incompatible score scales never have to be calibrated against each other.
The cross-encoder re-scores only the merged candidates, with full attention between query and passage. Simplified: real systems also add filters, caching and deduplication.

blocks.md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with a metric such as recall at k (the share of relevant passages that appear in the top k results).

Misconception: a higher similarity score means a more relevant passage across queries. Cosine scores are only comparable within one query's ranking and one model. A fixed threshold like 0.7 that works for one model can be meaningless for another.

blocks.question: A dense-only search works well on natural questions but users complain that searching an exact SKU like `KX-4471-B` returns similar-looking but wrong products. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase the embedding dimension from 384 to 1024
Lower the softmax temperature at query time
Switch from cosine to dot product
Add BM25 in parallel and fuse the lists with RRF
blocks.explain: Rare exact identifiers are where lexical matching is strongest and dense vectors are weakest. Hybrid retrieval keeps the dense model's paraphrase handling and adds exact-term recall. Temperature is a training-time setting; more dimensions or another similarity function do not create exact-match behavior.

blocks.question: In RRF with k = 60, document X is ranked 1st by BM25 and absent from the dense list. Document Y is ranked 3rd in both lists. Which ranks higher after fusion?
options: Y, because 2/63 is larger than 1/61
X, because a first place always wins
They tie
It depends on the raw BM25 score of X
blocks.explain: X gets 1/61, about 0.0164. Y gets 1/63 + 1/63, about 0.0317. RRF rewards agreement between retrievers, and it never looks at raw scores, so X's BM25 score is irrelevant.
